notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Header compression — RFC 7541: HPACK

  • Priority signalling, and its deprecation — RFC 9113 §5.3: Prioritization

  • Server push — RFC 9113 §8.4: Server Push

  • What replaced push — RFC 8297: An HTTP Status Code for Indicating Hints (103 Early Hints)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
HPACK's two tables? A fixed static table of 61 common entries, plus a per-connection dynamic table.
Status of RFC 7540 priorities? Deprecated by RFC 9113. Implemented inconsistently; largely unused.
Why did server push fail? The server can't know what the client has cached, so it pushed bytes that got discarded.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Three features ride on HTTP/2's framing layer, and they've had very different fates. HPACK compresses headers against a shared table, so a repeated cookie costs one byte instead of four hundred — that one is a clear, durable win. Stream priorities let a client express what to send first; they were implemented inconsistently and RFC 9113 deprecated the original scheme. Server push let a server send resources before they were asked for; it was abandoned because the server can't know what's already cached, and 103 Early Hints replaced the idea.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

How does HPACK actually get a 400-byte header down to one byte?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know it's indexed state rather than a compression algorithm like gzip.

Two tables and an index. The static table is fixed and shared by every HTTP/2 implementation — 61 entries of the most common header fields, some with values (:method: GET is index 2, :status: 200 is index 8). Referencing one costs a single byte. The dynamic table is built per connection as headers are seen: the first time you send cookie: session=abc..., it goes on the wire in full and both sides append it to their table; every subsequent request references it by index. A 400-byte cookie repeated across a hundred requests costs 400 bytes once and one byte ninety-nine times.

Values that don't repeat are Huffman-coded with a fixed table tuned for HTTP header characters, which saves roughly 20–30% on the literal. But the large win is indexing, not entropy coding, and that difference matters because it explains HPACK's one real constraint: the table is stateful and order-dependent. Header block N may reference an entry inserted by block N−1, so blocks must be processed in order. On TCP that's free, since TCP guarantees ordering anyway. On QUIC, where streams arrive out of order, it would reintroduce head-of-line blocking at the compression layer — which is exactly why HTTP/3 needed QPACK rather than simply reusing HPACK.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Server push had a sound theory. Why is it dead, and what should I say when asked?

📍 Seen in the wild: a favourite question because it's a rare, well-documented case of a shipped standard being withdrawn in practice.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can analyse a design failure rather than just report it.

The theory: the server knows the HTML references app.css, so instead of waiting a round trip for the browser to parse and request it, push it alongside. Saves an RTT on the critical path. The flaw is that the server does not know what the client already has cached. A returning visitor already holds app.css, so the push is pure waste — bytes sent, bandwidth spent, and on a constrained mobile link those bytes actively compete with resources the client genuinely needs. Cache digests were proposed to close the gap and never shipped, because they were complex and privacy-sensitive.

There were secondary problems that compounded it: push interacted badly with HTTP caching semantics, was hard to reason about across a CDN, and measurement repeatedly showed neutral or negative results in the field. Chrome removed support in 2022 and other browsers followed. The replacement is 103 Early Hints (RFC 8297), and the design lesson is in the difference: instead of pushing the resource, the server sends an interim response saying "you will want app.css", and the client decides whether to fetch it — checking its own cache first. Same round-trip saving on the critical path, no wasted bytes, and the decision sits with the party that has the information. When asked, that contrast is the answer: push failed because it put a decision on the side of the connection that lacked the facts.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Feature Status Why Use today
HPACK Alive, universal Large measured win; no downside Always on; tune table size only under memory pressure
RFC 7540 priorities Deprecated by RFC 9113 Complex tree model, inconsistent implementations Don't rely on it; some stacks use the simpler Priority header scheme
Server push Effectively dead Server can't know client cache state Don't propose it
103 Early Hints Alive, growing Client keeps the decision; no wasted bytes The correct answer when asked about push
QPACK Alive (HTTP/3) HPACK's ordering assumption breaks on QUIC Automatic; nothing to configure

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The arithmetic. 120 requests each carrying ~480 bytes of headers (cookie, user-agent, accept, referer). Uncompressed: 120 × 480 ≈ 58 KB, re-sent every page load, on the upload direction where mobile links are weakest. With HPACK: ~480 bytes for the first request, then 8–30 bytes each → ≈ 4 KB. Roughly a 14× reduction, and it lands on the scarce direction. This is a large part of HTTP/2's real-world win and it's often attributed to multiplexing instead.

The dynamic table defaults to 4,096 bytes per direction per connection (SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE). That's small — a handful of large cookies fill it — and entries are evicted FIFO when it overflows, so a workload with many distinct large headers gets less benefit than the arithmetic suggests. It's also a memory line item at scale: 50,000 connections × 4 KB × 2 directions is roughly 400 MB before any stream state exists.

Priorities were a dependency tree with weights — stream 5 depends on stream 3, weight 200 — and the model proved hard to implement consistently, with servers disagreeing about how to interpret it and clients rarely sending anything useful. RFC 9113 deprecated the signalling. A simpler scheme based on a Priority header with urgency and incremental fields is what implementations have moved toward, and the honest summary is that prioritisation in HTTP/2 mostly did not work as designed.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't propose server push. It's still in RFC 9113 but removed from Chrome and effectively dead. Suggesting it as a live optimisation dates an answer badly; 103 Early Hints is the current form of the idea.

  • Don't depend on HTTP/2 stream priorities for anything correctness-adjacent. The original scheme is deprecated and was never implemented consistently. If ordering matters, control it at the application layer — request the critical resources first — rather than trusting a priority signal.

  • Don't raise the HPACK table size reflexively. It's per direction per connection, so at high connection counts it multiplies into real memory, and the benefit flattens quickly once your common headers fit. Measure before raising it.

  • Don't let HPACK excuse large headers. It removes the cost of repetition, not of size. A 4 KB JWT still costs 4 KB the first time on every connection, and it evicts other entries from a 4 KB table while doing so.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "HPACK is gzip for headers."

✅ Reality: It's primarily an indexing scheme against a shared static and dynamic table — a repeated header becomes an index, not a compressed string. Huffman coding of literals is a secondary saving. The distinction matters because indexed state is what makes HPACK order-dependent, and that ordering assumption is precisely what forced QPACK's existence for HTTP/3.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I assumed HTTP/2's gains were essentially all multiplexing. On real pages with large cookies and auth headers, HPACK is a substantial share of the win — a 14× reduction on the upload direction, which on a mobile link is the constrained one. It's the least-discussed of HTTP/2's features and one of the two that actually survived.

  • 51-quic.md — where QPACK replaces HPACK, and why it had to

notes.html:
🧭 Scope note. The transport mechanism — why an ordered byte stream cannot deliver past a gap, the two recovery paths, the RTO floor — is owned by ../03-tcp-udp/25-tcp-head-of-line-blocking.md. This note owns the HTTP/2 consequence: what multiplexing promised, what the shared connection actually delivers, how to measure the gap on your own traffic, and how it decides an HTTP/3 migration. Read 25 first if the transport half is unfamiliar.

📚 Reference Links

  • HTTP/2's own statement of the limitation — RFC 9113 §5: Streams and Multiplexing

  • Measured HTTP/3 vs HTTP/2 under loss — Comparing HTTP/3 vs. HTTP/2 Performance

  • The transport that removes it — RFC 9000 §2: Streams

  • Why header compression had to be redesigned too — RFC 9204: QPACK

  • Bonus — the TCP-side treatment: High Performance Browser Networking: Head-of-Line Blocking

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What did HTTP/2 fix, precisely? Application-layer blocking only — the rule that responses return in request order.
Why can't TCP honour stream IDs? They live inside the byte stream TCP is refusing to deliver. TCP can't see them.
Did HTTP/2 make transport blocking better or worse? Worse. Six blast radii of 1/6 became one blast radius of 1.
Loss rate where HTTP/2 starts losing to HTTP/1.1? Around 2%. Below ~0.1% you'll never observe it.
What else on the connection is order-dependent? HPACK's dynamic table — which is why HTTP/3 needed QPACK, not just QUIC.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

HTTP/2 removed the application-layer blocking — a hundred streams now interleave freely on one connection. But those streams share one TCP byte stream, and TCP delivers strictly in order, so one lost packet stalls every stream on the connection regardless of which one it belonged to. Stream IDs are inside the bytes TCP is refusing to hand up; the transport cannot honour a distinction it cannot see. And by collapsing six connections into one, HTTP/2 made the blast radius bigger, not smaller — which is why above about 2% loss it can lose to HTTP/1.1.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

HTTP/2 frames are tagged with stream IDs. Why doesn't that let TCP deliver them independently?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can name the layering violation, or only assert that the problem persists.

Because the tags are payload. From TCP's perspective an HTTP/2 connection is one undifferentiated sequence of bytes; the 9-byte frame headers carrying the stream IDs are simply bytes at particular offsets within it. TCP's contract is that recv() returns bytes in stream order, so when a segment is missing, everything after the gap sits in the receive buffer undelivered — including the frame headers that would have said "this belongs to stream 47, which had no loss at all". The information needed to make a better decision exists, but it is on the wrong side of the boundary.

This is a clean layering problem rather than an implementation shortcoming, and that framing matters: no TCP option, no congestion control algorithm and no kernel tuning can fix it, because the fix requires the transport to understand application-layer structure. There were only two ways out — teach TCP about streams, which means changing kernels and middleboxes worldwide, or move to a transport that carries stream IDs in the packet where the transport can read them. QUIC took the second route, and every other QUIC design decision follows from that one.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

So did HTTP/2 make things better or worse? Six connections had blocking too.

📍 Seen in the wild: the sharpest version of this question, and the one that separates a memorised talking point from an understood trade.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can hold two true things at once — HTTP/2 is better on most paths and structurally worse on lossy ones.

Better on most paths, structurally worse on lossy ones, and the crossover is around 2% loss. HTTP/1.1's six connections were six independent TCP sequence spaces, so a lost packet stalled roughly one sixth of in-flight work while the other five lanes kept moving. That's accidental fault isolation, bought at the price of six handshakes, six cold congestion windows and six congestion controllers competing on one bottleneck. HTTP/2 consolidates all of it: one handshake, one warm window, proper prioritisation, header compression — and one shared failure domain where a single lost packet stalls all hundred streams.

So HTTP/2 traded many small blocking domains for one large one, and bet that loss would be rare. On a fixed-line connection at 0.01% loss that bet pays enormously and the stall is never observed. On a congested mobile network at 2%+ it starts to lose, and the loss is concentrated in exactly the users who were already having the worst experience. The honest framing in a design discussion is that HTTP/2 is the right default and its weakness is a tail phenomenon affecting a segment — which is also precisely why HTTP/3's benefit shows up as a p99 improvement in a mobile cohort rather than as a change in your aggregate dashboard.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

You run HTTP/2 for 10 million mobile users. How do you know whether this is costing you anything?

📍 Seen in the wild: the measurement question, which is where most people's answer runs out.

What runs out is not a resource but visibility, and that's the trap. Head-of-line blocking never moves the median, because most requests experience no loss; it produces a tail. Aggregate p50 and mean latency look identical whether this is costing you nothing or costing a fifth of your users a second per stall, so the standard dashboard is structurally incapable of detecting it. The measurement has to be built deliberately.

Three signals, in order of directness. Segment p99 latency by network type (cellular versus Wi-Fi versus fixed) and by country — if HTTP/2 blocking is real for you, the cellular cohort's p99 diverges from its p50 far more than the fixed cohort's does. Chart the distribution, not percentiles alone: transport-induced stalls cluster at recognisable values, and a spike sitting at roughly one second is the Linux RTO floor wearing a disguise, which is diagnostic. Correlate with server-side retransmission counters (ss -ti retrans, TcpRetransSegs) on the terminating tier, because that separates a transport stall from a slow backend, a buffering proxy or client-side rendering — all of which produce a similar user-visible symptom. The operational failure mode is subtler than the technical one: teams enable HTTP/3, see no movement in the aggregate, and conclude it did nothing, when the win was concentrated in a cohort they never separated out.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

You're deciding whether to run HTTP/3 at the edge. Make the case, and say what it costs.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can justify a platform change with a measurement rather than a vendor claim.

The highest-stakes constraint is that this is a tail-latency improvement for a subset of users, so the business case has to be made on that subset's size, not on an average that will barely move. Start by measuring: segment p99 by network type for a week. If your cellular and high-RTT international cohorts show a p99/p50 ratio much worse than your fixed-line cohort, and retransmission counters confirm it's transport rather than backend, the win is real and quantifiable. If your traffic is desktop clients on good networks, HTTP/3 buys close to nothing and the honest recommendation is to skip it — which is a stronger answer than advocating for it unconditionally.

The topology, if you proceed: client → anycast edge PoP terminating HTTP/3 over QUIC, advertising itself via Alt-Svc with HTTP/2 over TCP as the fallback, then a pooled HTTP/2 connection over the provider backbone to a regional origin. Note that the backhaul stays on HTTP/2 deliberately — loss on a backbone path is negligible, so per-stream recovery buys nothing there, and TCP is simpler to operate. Edge placement is doing double duty: it shortens the lossy leg and shrinks the RTT that the RTO is computed from, so even the stalls that remain are cheaper.

The costs to name honestly, because they're what a reviewer will push on. UDP must traverse your load balancers and firewalls, which for many organisations means a different LB product (an NLB rather than an ALB, or a QUIC-capable edge). You are now operating two protocol paths, and every debugging session starts with "which one was this user on?". QUIC's transport headers are largely encrypted, so the tcpdump-based loss diagnosis from Tier 3 no longer works the same way and you need QUIC-aware tooling and qlog. And the fallback path must be monitored: if a firewall blocks UDP and most traffic quietly rides HTTP/2, you have paid the operational cost and received none of the benefit — that ratio, HTTP/3 versus fallback share, is the first thing I'd alert on.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Stack App-layer blocking Transport-layer blocking Blast radius of one lost packet Where it wins
HTTP/1.1, 1 connection Yes — strict response order Yes That connection's queue Nowhere; the baseline
HTTP/1.1, 6 connections Yes, per connection Yes, per connection ~1/6 of in-flight work Above ~2% loss, accidentally
HTTP/1.1 pipelining Yes — server must respond in order Yes The whole pipeline Nowhere; abandoned
HTTP/2 over TCP No Yes, connection-wide All streams Clean paths, which is most paths
HTTP/3 over QUIC No Per-stream only The one stream that lost it Lossy and high-RTT paths
HTTP/3, within one stream No Yes, inside that stream That stream Unavoidable — ordering is still promised per stream

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

The labels are inside the sealed crate.

📖 Story

You pack a hundred labelled parcels into one shipping crate. The freight company's rule is that crates are opened strictly in order, so when crate two goes missing, crates three onward sit on the dock unopened — and the labels that would prove ninety-nine of those parcels have nothing to do with the missing crate are inside crates nobody is allowed to open yet.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • Labelled parcels = HTTP/2 frames tagged with stream IDs

  • The sealed crate opened strictly in order = TCP's ordered byte-stream delivery

  • Labels inside the unopened crates = stream IDs living in the payload, invisible to the transport

  • Ninety-nine unrelated parcels stuck = every other stream stalled by a loss that wasn't theirs

  • Putting the label on the outside of each crate = QUIC carrying stream IDs in the packet, where the transport can read them

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The diagram is the whole argument, and the load-bearing line is "the HTTP/2 layer sees nothing". Multiplexing is implemented one layer above the layer that decides what gets delivered, and the deciding layer has no access to the multiplexing information. The mechanism detail — three duplicate ACKs versus the RTO path, and why the second is fifty times worse — belongs to ../03-tcp-udp/25-tcp-head-of-line-blocking.md; what matters here is the amplification factor that HTTP/2 adds on top.

Blast radius arithmetic. With n independent connections and s streams total, one lost packet stalls s ÷ n streams.

HTTP/1.1, 6 connections, 120 requests: 120 ÷ 6 = 20 requests stalled. HTTP/2, 1 connection, 120 requests: 120 ÷ 1 = 120 requests stalled. HTTP/3, per-stream recovery: 1 request stalled.

HTTP/2's multiplexing win and its blocking loss come from the same consolidation. You cannot have one without the other on TCP.

There is a second, subtler order dependency that people miss and that explains why HTTP/3 needed more than just QUIC. HPACK's dynamic table is stateful and order-sensitive: header block N may reference a table entry inserted by header block N−1, so headers must be processed in the order they were sent. That's fine on TCP, which guarantees ordering anyway. Put HPACK on a transport that delivers streams out of order and it breaks — which is exactly why RFC 9204 defines QPACK, a redesign that tolerates out-of-order delivery using separate encoder and decoder instruction streams. If HTTP/3 had kept HPACK, it would have reintroduced head-of-line blocking at the header-compression layer and undone the point of the exercise.

Finally, note what HTTP/3 does not remove: blocking within a single stream. A stream still promises ordered delivery of its own bytes, so a loss inside a large response still stalls that response. The guarantee moved from per-connection to per-stream, which is a large practical win and not an elimination.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is p99 latency segmented by network conditions, and the reason this topic earns a CORE note is that the aggregate number is actively misleading. Head-of-line blocking never touches the median, so a service can be costing a cellular cohort a second per stall while every dashboard reads green. The metric that exposes it is the p99/p50 ratio compared across network types — a fixed-line cohort and a cellular cohort should have similar ratios if the transport isn't the problem, and a diverging ratio is the signal.

The second reason it matters is that it's the whole decision procedure for HTTP/3 adoption. HTTP/3 is a platform change with real operational cost — UDP through your infrastructure, two protocol paths, new tooling — and its benefit is concentrated entirely in the cohort this note describes. Being able to say "we measured a 2.3× p99/p50 ratio on cellular against 1.2× on fixed, and retransmission counters confirm transport" is what turns that from a vendor claim into a decision.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# 1. Reproduce it deliberately. 2% loss is the documented crossover point.
sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem loss 2% delay 50ms

# 2. Same page, same server, both protocol versions, under that loss.
for v in --http1.1 --http2; do
  curl $v -s -o /dev/null -w "$v  ver:%{http_version}  total:%{time_total}\n" \
       https://example.com/heavy-page
done
sudo tc qdisc del dev eth0 root

# 3. Is this connection actually retransmitting? The evidence that separates
#    a transport stall from a slow backend or a buffering proxy.
ss -ti state established '( dport = :443 )' | grep -E 'retrans|rto|rtt|cwnd'

# 4. Server-side rate over an interval — sample twice, don't read once.
nstat -az TcpRetransSegs TcpExtTCPTimeouts TcpExtTCPLostRetransmit

# 5. Offer HTTP/3 with an HTTP/2 fallback. Alt-Svc is how the client learns.
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen 443 quic reuseport;          # UDP listener — must be open end to end
    http2 on;

    # Advertise h3 for 24h; the client upgrades on its NEXT connection, not this one
    add_header Alt-Svc 'h3=":443"; ma=86400' always;
}

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

The same page from example.com under the netem conditions above — 50ms RTT, 2% loss, 120 assets:

📥 t=0ms       HTTP/2, one connection, 120 streams opened
    │
    ▼
⚙️ [1] 120 HEADERS sent, DATA frames interleaving normally   t=100-800ms
    │
    ▼
❌ [2] one segment lost — carried frames for stream 37       t=840ms
    │
    ▼
⚠️ [3] frames for streams 1, 5, 9 ... 239 arrive             t=840-1890ms
    │       all buffered by TCP, none delivered to HTTP/2
    │       119 streams stalled by a loss on the 120th
    ▼
⏱️ [4] recovery — dup ACKs available, fast retransmit         +50ms (1 RTT)
    │       had this been a tail loss: +1000ms (RTO floor)
    ▼
✅ [5] gap filled, ~40 buffered frames delivered at once      t=890ms
    │       burst arrival, visible as a waterfall staircase
    ▼
🎯 [6] Page complete                                          t=2400ms

--- same page, same loss, HTTP/3 ---
❌ [7] equivalent packet lost, carried stream 37 only         t=840ms
✅ [8] streams 1, 5, 9 ... continue uninterrupted             t=840ms+
🎯 [9] Page complete                                          t=1650ms
        Only stream 37 waited. 31% faster, entirely from the tail.

[1] Steady state is HTTP/2 at its best: 120 concurrent streams, one warm congestion window, headers compressed. Nothing here would motivate a migration.

[2] One packet lost. It happened to carry frames for stream 37 — a fact TCP does not know and could not act on if it did.

[3] This is the note. 119 streams that lost nothing are held in the receive buffer for a full round trip, because the bytes that identify them sit behind the gap. In the browser waterfall this appears as every in-flight request's bar extending simultaneously — a distinctive staircase that, once you've seen it, is unmistakable.

[4] Recovery here takes the cheap path: with 120 streams active there is plenty of data in flight to generate three duplicate ACKs, so fast retransmit fires within a round trip. Note the contrast with a token stream, where sparse traffic means no duplicate ACKs and the stall becomes the 1-second RTO floor instead — the same mechanism, fifty times more expensive.

[5] The gap fills and roughly forty buffered frames are delivered in one burst. The bytes were on the machine the whole time; only the delivery contract held them.

[6–9] 2400ms versus 1650ms on identical bytes and an identical server. The entire 31% is tail behaviour — and on a clean path the same comparison shows the two versions within noise of each other, which is why this must be measured under representative conditions rather than in a datacentre.

10. When TO Use This

This is a limitation rather than a technique, so the question is when accepting it is right:

  • Accept it whenever loss is genuinely negligible. Inside a datacentre, over a cloud backbone, on office fixed-line connections — well under 0.1% loss means the stall is never observed and HTTP/2's consolidation is pure win. Most backend-to-backend traffic is in this category.

  • Accept it when your clients can't reach you over UDP. If a meaningful share of your users sit behind firewalls that block UDP, HTTP/3 is a fallback path that rarely activates and you've paid operational cost for nothing.

  • Accept it while you're measuring. Enabling HTTP/3 before you can segment p99 by network type means you won't be able to tell whether it helped, which makes the change unjustifiable either way.

  • Design around it when the workload is small, frequent writes over a consumer network. Token streaming, live updates, chat. That's the traffic shape that misses fast retransmit and lands on the RTO floor, and it's where HTTP/3 earns its complexity most clearly.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't deploy HTTP/2 with high stream concurrency across a lossy long-haul path without weighing HTTP/3. The degradation isn't gradual — below ~1% loss you see nothing, above ~2% the tail falls apart because every stream shares every stall. It reads on dashboards as a backend problem and isn't.

  • Don't migrate to HTTP/3 before ruling out the impostors. A buffering proxy, a slow upstream and client-side rendering all produce a similar bursty symptom, and all three are more common than transport blocking. proxy_buffering off costs a config line to test; HTTP/3 is a platform project. Check the cheap thing first.

  • Don't shard across parallel HTTP/2 connections as your fix. It's HTTP/1.1's workaround in modern clothing: you regain fault isolation and pay for it with multiple handshakes, cold windows, split HPACK contexts and competing congestion controllers. Below about four connections it's occasionally defensible; beyond that you usually make the tail worse.

  • Don't tune tcp_rto_min to soften the stalls. A too-eager timer fires on paths whose RTT estimate is briefly wrong, adding retransmissions exactly when the network is struggling. The legitimate levers are shortening the path and changing transport.

  • Don't claim HTTP/3 percentages without conditions. "30% faster" invites an immediate and fair challenge. The defensible form names the loss regime and the cohort, and cites your own measurement.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "HTTP/2 fixed head-of-line blocking."

✅ Reality: It fixed the application-layer form — HTTP/1.1's rule that responses return in request order. The transport-layer form remains and is structurally worse, because collapsing six connections into one means a lost packet now stalls every stream rather than a sixth of them. Stating it without that qualification is the single most common wrong claim about the protocol.

❌ Misconception: "HTTP/3 eliminates head-of-line blocking."

✅ Reality: It eliminates the connection-wide form. Within a single stream, ordered delivery is still promised, so a loss inside one large response still stalls that response. QPACK also has to be careful, since header-table dependencies could otherwise reintroduce blocking at the compression layer. The guarantee moved from per-connection to per-stream — a large win, not an elimination.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I assumed HTTP/2's remaining blocking was a rough edge that a smarter TCP stack or better congestion control would eventually smooth over. It can't be: the transport would have to understand application-layer framing, and it structurally cannot, because the framing lives in the bytes it's withholding. That's why the industry built an entire new transport rather than patching the existing one — and once I saw it as a layering boundary rather than an implementation gap, QUIC stopped looking like over-engineering.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Stating "HTTP/2 fixed head-of-line blocking" flat. This is the trap the topic exists to catch. Always name which layer, and volunteer that the transport-layer form got worse — that one qualification is usually what's being tested.

Describing it as a loss-recovery inefficiency. It's not a performance defect awaiting a tuning fix; it's a consequence of the ordered-delivery contract. Framing it as inefficiency leads to answers about sysctls, when the real answers are architectural — shorten the path, or change transport.

Advocating HTTP/3 without a measurement. The strong answer is conditional: name the loss regime where the benefit appears, name the cohort you'd segment, and say you'd skip it if the numbers don't show up. Unconditional advocacy reads as repeating a vendor blog.

Ignoring the middle of the path. In production, "my responses arrive in bursts" is a buffering proxy far more often than transport blocking. An answer that jumps to QUIC without mentioning proxy_buffering is describing a two-endpoint world.

Forgetting QPACK. If asked why HTTP/3 couldn't just run HPACK over QUIC, the answer is that HPACK's dynamic table assumes total ordering across streams, which is precisely what QUIC removes. Knowing that shows you understand the change went deeper than swapping transports.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Loss rate where HTTP/2 degrades vs HTTP/1.1 ~2% Where one shared connection loses to six independent ones Cloudflare HTTP/3 vs HTTP/2
Blast radius, HTTP/1.1 6 connections ~1/6 of in-flight requests Accidental isolation from parallel connections Derived
Blast radius, HTTP/2 All streams on the connection The cost of consolidation RFC 9113 §5
Blast radius, HTTP/3 1 stream Stream IDs carried in the packet RFC 9000 §2
Stall on fast retransmit ~1 RTT Requires 3 duplicate ACKs, so requires data in flight RFC 5681 §3.2
Stall on RTO path 1 second (Linux floor) Sparse traffic generates no duplicate ACKs RFC 6298 §2.4
HTTP/3 ALPN token h3 Negotiated in TLS; Alt-Svc is how clients discover it RFC 9114 §3.2
HPACK default table size 4,096 bytes Order-dependent, which is why QPACK exists RFC 7541 §4.2

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Consolidation removes per-request serialisation and concentrates every stall; the trade is median against tail
💰 Cost One connection is cheaper in handshakes and server state — the saving you hand back if you shard for isolation
🔒 Security / visibility QUIC encrypts most transport headers, so the tcpdump retransmission diagnosis used here doesn't transfer; you need qlog and QUIC-aware tooling
📈 Scale Blast radius scales with multiplexing depth — 100 streams per connection means one packet can stall 100 units of work
🔧 Ops complexity HTTP/3 means UDP through LBs and firewalls, a fallback path to monitor, and two protocols to debug, against a tail-only benefit
🐛 Debuggability The symptom is indistinguishable from a buffering proxy, a slow upstream or client rendering; separating them needs retransmission counters, not intuition

16. Real World Usage

QUIC exists because of this specific problem. Google's measurements on lossy mobile networks showed SPDY/HTTP/2's multiplexing being undermined by transport blocking, and concluded that fixing TCP was impossible on any useful timescale — TCP lives in kernels and middleboxes that take a decade to turn over. Building a new transport on UDP was the faster path, which makes this as much a deployment-velocity story as a protocol-design one.

gRPC across regions is where backend teams meet it. Many RPCs multiplex onto one long-lived connection, so a single lost packet delays every in-flight call between two services. Intra-datacentre it's invisible; across regions or over a VPN it produces correlated latency spikes across unrelated calls, which is a genuinely confusing thing to debug because the affected requests share nothing except a connection.

LLM token streaming is the current high-profile case. Small frequent writes over consumer networks is exactly the traffic shape that misses fast retransmit and lands on the RTO floor, which is why streaming products care about HTTP/3 far more than page-load products ever did.

17. Acronym Decoder

  • QPACK — QUIC-friendly header compression, RFC 9204. HPACK's dynamic table assumes a total ordering across streams; QUIC removes that ordering, so QPACK re-does the compression with separate encoder and decoder instruction streams and explicit blocked-stream handling. Its existence is proof that removing head-of-line blocking required changes above the transport as well as at it.

  • RTO — Retransmission Timeout. The expensive recovery path, taken when there is too little data in flight to produce three duplicate ACKs, floored at one second on Linux.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • ../03-tcp-udp/25-tcp-head-of-line-blocking.md — the transport mechanism this note builds on; read it first

  • 48-http2-binary-framing.md — the streams whose independence TCP cannot honour

  • 46-http11-limits.md — the application-layer blocking that HTTP/2 genuinely did fix

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 51-quic.md — the transport built to remove this, and why stream IDs moved into the packet

  • 53-http3-semantics-over-quic.md — what changed and what didn't when HTTP moved onto QUIC

  • 54-when-each-version-matters.md — the decision framework this note supplies the evidence for

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Sharding across parallel HTTP/2 connections — regains isolation, pays for it in handshakes, cold windows and split HPACK contexts

  • Edge termination — doesn't remove the blocking, shortens the leg it happens on and shrinks the RTO with the RTT

  • Accepting it — correct on any low-loss path, which is most backend traffic

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Alt-Svc and ALPN — how a client discovers and selects HTTP/3, and how the fallback stays available

  • Buffering proxies — produce an identical symptom for a different reason; always excluded first

  • Congestion control — determines how much data is in flight, which decides whether a stall costs 1 RTT or 1 second

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

Usually as a debugging scenario before it's a design one: "your page loads fine in the office and badly for mobile users in another region — walk me through it." What's being tested is whether you enumerate candidates in cost order (buffering proxy, then transport blocking, then client rendering), name the measurement that separates them, and only then propose a change. The design question follows immediately — "now design the delivery path so this stops mattering" — where edge placement and protocol selection are the answer.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10k users, mostly fixed-line Nothing transport-related; blocking affects a small cellular slice Ship HTTP/2, disable proxy buffering, build the p99-by-network measurement before spending more
1M users, third on mobile Long-haul RTT inflates every stall; the affected cohort is now large enough to matter commercially Edge PoPs to shorten the lossy leg; enable HTTP/3 with a monitored fallback
10M users, global Two protocol paths at every PoP, UDP capacity through the edge, tooling gap for QUIC debugging QUIC-capable edge fleet, qlog sampling, per-cohort SLOs, connection-level metrics per version

The cost dimension is that HTTP/3 adds edge fleet capability, possibly a different load-balancer product for UDP, and a second debugging discipline. All of it is justified by tail latency for a segment, so the case must be built on that segment's size and value — an aggregate average will show almost no change and will not carry the argument.

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • At 10x: p99 develops a cluster near the RTO floor for cellular users while p50 stays flat — invisible on any average-based dashboard.

  • At 100x: correlated stalls across unrelated streams sharing a connection, so latency spikes look like a backend fault and get routed to the wrong team.

  • Operationally: a firewall blocks UDP and most traffic quietly rides the HTTP/2 fallback. Both paths "work", nobody notices, and the tail-latency win you paid for was never delivered.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • p99/p50 latency ratio, segmented by network type and HTTP version. The single metric that makes this topic observable. Alert on divergence between cohorts, not on absolute p99.

  • TCP retransmission rate per connection (ss -ti, TcpRetransSegs) at the terminating tier — the evidence separating a transport stall from a buffering proxy or a slow backend.

  • Share of traffic on HTTP/3 versus the fallback. If HTTP/3 was adopted for tail latency, this ratio is the measurement of whether you actually received it. A quiet collapse to fallback is the failure mode most likely to go unnoticed.

📚 Reference Links

🚀 REVISION BLOCK (Sections 1–5)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Handshake cost, new connection vs resumed? 1 RTT (transport + crypto together); 0-RTT on resumption, at replay risk.
The one design decision everything follows from? Stream IDs live in the packet, so the transport can recover per stream.
Why UDP and not a new IP protocol? Middleboxes. UDP is the only thing that reliably traverses the internet's installed base.
What identifies a QUIC connection? A connection ID, not the 4-tuple — which is what makes migration possible.
Where does QUIC live? Userspace, in the application. That's why it ships without waiting for kernels.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

QUIC is a transport that rebuilds everything TCP gives you — reliability, ordering, congestion control — on top of UDP, in userspace, with TLS 1.3 fused in rather than layered on. Two consequences matter. Setup collapses to one round trip because transport and crypto negotiate together, and zero on resumption. And stream IDs live in the packet header rather than inside the byte stream, so a lost packet stalls only its own stream instead of all of them. UDP isn't chosen for speed — it's the only substrate middleboxes reliably pass.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

QUIC re-implements reliability and congestion control. So why build it on UDP at all?

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand this as a deployability decision rather than a performance one.

Because UDP is a delivery mechanism, not a design endorsement. QUIC needs packets carried end to end with a port number for demultiplexing and nothing else — everything above that it does itself. It could in principle have been a new IP protocol number, which would have been cleaner. It wasn't, because the internet's installed base of NATs, firewalls and middleboxes drops anything that isn't TCP or UDP, and a protocol that fails on a third of networks is not deployable regardless of its merits.

The second half of the answer is where the protocol lives. TCP is in the kernel, so improving it means shipping kernel updates across every OS, every mobile device and every middlebox that inspects TCP options — a decade-scale problem, and the reason TCP Fast Open never achieved broad adoption despite being standardised. QUIC runs in userspace as a library inside the application, so a browser can ship a new congestion controller in a six-week release cycle and a server operator can upgrade by deploying a binary. That agility is arguably the biggest thing QUIC bought, and it's the part people most often miss because it isn't a protocol feature at all.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

0-RTT sounds free. What does it actually cost, and when would you refuse it?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard probe once someone mentions 0-RTT; the wrong answer is treating it as strictly better.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know that 0-RTT trades a security property for a round trip, and can name which requests may make that trade.

0-RTT lets a returning client send application data in its very first flight, using keys derived from a previous session. The cost is that this data has no replay protection. An attacker who captures that first flight can resend it later, and the server cannot distinguish the replay from the original — there has been no round trip yet, so no freshness has been established. TLS 1.3 has the same property for the same reason; QUIC inherits it.

So the rule is that 0-RTT data must be idempotent and non-state-changing. A GET for a cached article is fine — replaying it wastes a little work and reveals nothing new. A POST /transfer is not, and neither is anything that consumes a one-time token or increments a counter. In practice you configure the edge to accept 0-RTT only for safe methods and to reject or defer anything else to the 1-RTT path, which is what mainstream CDN implementations do by default. It's also worth naming that 0-RTT data can be exposed to a forward-secrecy gap, which is a second reason to keep sensitive payloads off it. The design answer is that 0-RTT is a per-request decision, not a per-connection setting — and treating it as a global speed switch is how it becomes a correctness bug.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

You put QUIC behind your edge at high volume. What runs out or breaks first?

📍 Seen in the wild: the operations-side question, and the one that decides whether an HTTP/3 rollout succeeds.

CPU, and specifically per-packet CPU in userspace. TCP's per-packet work happens in the kernel with decades of optimisation behind it — segmentation offload, checksum offload, GRO/GSO batching, and a receive path that has been tuned since the 1990s. QUIC processes each datagram in userspace, doing its own packet-number decoding, decryption and ACK handling per packet, and early deployments commonly measured roughly 2–3× the CPU per byte compared with TCP. The gap has narrowed with UDP segmentation offload (UDP_SEGMENT), kernel GSO/GRO support for UDP, and careful implementation, but it hasn't closed, and it means an HTTP/3 edge fleet is sized differently from an HTTP/2 one.

It presents as CPU saturation at the edge under a traffic mix shift rather than a traffic volume increase — the day a popular mobile client enables HTTP/3 by default, your edge CPU rises with no change in request rate, which defeats the usual capacity model. Two secondary limits follow. UDP receive buffers (net.core.rmem_max) need raising, because the default is tuned for DNS-scale traffic and drops silently under load with only RcvbufErrors to show for it. And your load balancer must route by connection ID rather than 4-tuple, or migration and NAT rebinding break — a QUIC-unaware L4 balancer will send a migrated client's packets to a different backend that has no state for them. Monitor edge CPU per gigabit segmented by protocol version, and netstat -su receive errors.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design an HTTP/3 rollout for a global consumer product. Sequence it and say what you'd watch.

🎯 Really testing: whether you treat this as a staged infrastructure programme with a measurable hypothesis, or as a config flag.

The dominating constraint is that HTTP/3's benefit is concentrated in a cohort and its cost is spread across the whole platform, so the rollout has to prove the benefit on a slice before paying the cost everywhere. Sequence it that way. First, build the measurement: p99 and p50 segmented by network type, region and negotiated HTTP version. Without that you cannot tell success from noise, because the aggregate will barely move either way. Then enable QUIC on a single edge PoP serving a mobile-heavy region, advertise Alt-Svc with a short ma so you can withdraw it quickly, and compare cohorts.

The topology: client → anycast edge PoP terminating QUIC (UDP 443 open end to end, LB routing by connection ID) → pooled HTTP/2 over TCP across the backbone → regional origin. The backhaul deliberately stays on TCP — backbone loss is negligible, so per-stream recovery buys nothing there, and TCP is cheaper in CPU and easier to debug. Alt-Svc is the discovery mechanism and it's worth being precise about it: the client learns about h3 from a header on an HTTP/2 response and upgrades on its next connection, so rollout and rollback both have a propagation delay bounded by the ma value you set.

Three failure modes to watch, in priority order. Silent fallback: a firewall blocks UDP, clients quietly ride HTTP/2, and you've paid the cost with no benefit — alert on the h3-versus-fallback share per region, because this one is invisible in every other metric. Edge CPU per gigabit by version, since the userspace packet cost is the capacity surprise. And connection-ID routing correctness — if migrated connections break, the symptom is elevated errors specifically for users switching networks, which looks like client flakiness and is not. The rollback lever is withdrawing Alt-Svc, which is clean but takes as long as the ma you advertised, so keep it short until you're confident.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Property TCP + TLS 1.3 + HTTP/2 QUIC + HTTP/3 Why it matters
Handshake to first byte 2 RTT (1 TCP + 1 TLS) 1 RTT, or 0 on resumption Halves setup on every new connection
Where it runs Kernel (TCP) + userspace (TLS) Entirely userspace Ships at application speed, not kernel speed
Loss recovery scope Whole connection Per stream The reason it exists
Connection identity 4-tuple Connection ID Survives IP change — Wi-Fi to cellular
Header compression HPACK (order-dependent) QPACK (out-of-order tolerant) HPACK would reintroduce blocking on QUIC
Encryption scope Payload; TCP headers in clear Payload and most transport headers Ossification resistance; also blinds your tooling
CPU per byte Lower — kernel, offloads Roughly 2–3× early on, narrowing Real capacity-planning consequence
Middlebox traversal Universal UDP often blocked Requires a monitored TCP fallback

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

🪝 Hook

Put the label on the outside of the crate.

📖 Story

The freight company kept crates sealed and opened them strictly in order, so one missing crate held up everything behind it. So you stopped using their crates: you write the parcel's number on the outside of each box, and now a missing box holds up only the parcel it belonged to. You also stopped negotiating the shipping contract and the security seal in two separate meetings — one meeting now does both.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • The number on the outside of the box = the stream ID in the QUIC packet header, visible to the transport

  • A missing box holds up only its parcel = per-stream loss recovery

  • Their crates versus yours = TCP in the kernel versus QUIC in userspace, which is why you could change it at all

  • One meeting instead of two = transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes fused into a single 1-RTT exchange

📖 DEPTH BLOCK (Sections 6–19)

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Four mechanisms carry the design.

Fused handshake. QUIC's transport parameters and the TLS 1.3 handshake travel in the same flight, so there is no "establish transport, then establish crypto" sequence. One round trip yields an encrypted, ready connection; on resumption, cached parameters plus a session ticket allow 0-RTT. TLS is not optional — there is no unencrypted QUIC, which removed a whole category of downgrade and middlebox-tampering problems by construction.

Per-stream recovery. A QUIC packet carries frames, and STREAM frames name their stream in the packet itself. When a packet is lost, the transport knows precisely which streams are affected and delivers every other stream normally. This is the entire architectural difference from HTTP/2 on TCP, where the stream IDs are inside the byte stream being withheld.

Packet numbers are monotonic and separate from stream offsets. TCP reuses the sequence number of a lost segment when retransmitting, which creates the classic retransmission ambiguity — an ACK could be for the original or the copy, so RTT samples get corrupted. QUIC assigns every packet, including retransmissions, a fresh monotonically increasing packet number, and carries the data's position separately as a stream offset. RTT measurement becomes unambiguous, which makes loss detection and congestion control measurably better. This is a small-sounding detail that senior engineers use as a depth probe.

Connection IDs. A connection is identified by an ID in the header, not by the 4-tuple, so a client whose IP or port changes — Wi-Fi to cellular, NAT rebinding — continues the same connection with no new handshake.

QUIC short header (1-RTT packets) — RFC 9000 §17.3

 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
|0|1|S|R|R|K|P P|      ← header form, spin bit, key phase, packet number length
+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
|  Destination Connection ID (0..160 bits)  |   ← identity, NOT the 4-tuple
+-------------------------------------------+
|     Packet Number (8..32 bits)            |   ← monotonic, never reused
+-------------------------------------------+
|     Protected Payload (STREAM frames...)  |   ← stream IDs live in here,
+-------------------------------------------+      readable by the transport

📚 Adapted from RFC 9000 §17.3. Almost everything after the first byte is encrypted or authenticated — deliberate ossification resistance, so middleboxes cannot come to depend on fields and freeze the protocol the way they froze TCP. The operational cost is that your packet-capture tooling can no longer read loss and retransmission behaviour without keys.

Setup arithmetic on a 200ms path. TCP + TLS 1.3 + HTTP/2: 1 RTT (TCP) + 1 RTT (TLS) = 400ms to first request byte. QUIC + HTTP/3, new connection: 1 RTT = 200ms. QUIC + HTTP/3, resumed with 0-RTT: 0ms — request data rides the first flight. On a resumed connection the setup term disappears entirely, which is why the benefit is largest for clients that reconnect often — exactly mobile clients.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is time to first byte on new connections, and p99 latency for lossy-network cohorts. QUIC attacks both halves of what makes a cold request slow: it halves the handshake (or removes it on resumption), and it stops one lost packet from stalling everything. Those are the two largest terms in a mobile client's request latency, which is why the measured benefit is concentrated there and close to nil on a fast fixed-line connection.

The second production observable is one people don't expect: edge CPU per gigabit. Moving packet processing from a heavily-optimised kernel path into userspace costs real cycles, and the day a major client enables HTTP/3 your edge CPU changes without any change in request rate. Capacity models keyed to requests per second stop predicting correctly, which makes this a planning problem as much as a performance one.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# 1. Did HTTP/3 actually negotiate? --http3 forces it; ALPN token is h3.
curl --http3 -sI https://cloudflare.com/ -o /dev/null \
     -w 'version:%{http_version}  total:%{time_total}\n'

# 2. Is the origin advertising it? Alt-Svc is how clients discover h3.
curl -sI https://cloudflare.com/ | grep -i alt-svc

# 3. UDP receive buffers — the silent-drop limit from Tier 3.
sysctl net.core.rmem_max net.core.rmem_default
netstat -su | grep -E 'receive buffer errors|packet receive errors'

# 4. Server side. Note listen 443 TWICE — TCP and UDP are separate listeners.
server {
    listen 443 ssl;                      # TCP: HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 fallback
    listen 443 quic reuseport;           # UDP: HTTP/3. Firewall must pass this.
    http2 on;

    ssl_early_data on;                   # 0-RTT — see the Tier 2 caveat
    # Advertise h3. Clients upgrade on their NEXT connection, so `ma` bounds
    # both rollout and rollback time. Keep it short until you're confident.
    add_header Alt-Svc 'h3=":443"; ma=3600' always;
}

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

A returning mobile client fetching a page from an edge PoP, 60ms RTT, ~1.5% loss:

📥 t=0ms       Client has a cached session ticket from an earlier visit
    │
    ▼
🔑 [1] Initial packet: 0-RTT keys + HTTP/3 GET, same flight   t=0ms
    │       no handshake wait — request data in the first packet
    ▼
🏛️ [2] Server accepts 0-RTT (safe method), begins response    t=60ms
    │       TTFB = 60ms = exactly 1 one-way + 1 one-way
    ▼
📡 [3] Response streams 0, 4, 8, 12 ... interleaved            t=60-400ms
    │
    ▼
❌ [4] packet lost — carried STREAM frames for stream 8        t=210ms
    │
    ▼
✅ [5] streams 0, 4, 12 continue delivering, uninterrupted     t=210ms
    │       transport reads the stream ID from the packet header
    ▼
🔄 [6] stream 8 retransmitted, NEW packet number               t=270ms
    │       unambiguous RTT sample — no retransmission ambiguity
    ▼
📶 [7] client moves Wi-Fi to cellular, source IP changes       t=320ms
    │       same connection ID → path validation, no new handshake
    ▼
🎯 [8] Page complete                                           t=520ms

--- same client, same conditions, HTTP/2 over TCP ---
🔒 [9]  TCP + TLS handshake                                    t=120ms (2 RTT)
⚠️ [10] equivalent loss stalls ALL streams for 1 RTT           +60ms
🚫 [11] network switch kills the connection, full re-handshake  +120ms
🎯 [12] Page complete                                          t=880ms

[1] 0-RTT is doing real work here: the request leaves in the very first packet. This is a GET, which is why accepting it is safe — a POST would be deferred to the 1-RTT path per the Tier 2 rule.

[2] TTFB of 60ms is one round trip total, with no separate transport and crypto phases. The HTTP/2 comparison at [9] spends 120ms before the request is even sent.

[4–5] The note's whole point in two lines. The lost packet carried stream 8's frames; the transport reads that from the packet header and delivers streams 0, 4 and 12 without interruption. On HTTP/2 ([10]) the same loss stalls every stream for a full RTT.

[6] The retransmission uses a fresh packet number, so when the ACK arrives the sender knows unambiguously which transmission it acknowledges. TCP cannot do this, and the resulting RTT sample corruption is a real (if second-order) reason QUIC's loss detection behaves better.

[7] The network switch is invisible. Because identity is the connection ID rather than the 4-tuple, the client validates the new path and continues — where TCP ([11]) must tear down and re-handshake, costing 2 RTTs and any in-flight requests.

[8] 520ms versus 880ms, same bytes and same server. Roughly a third of the gap is the handshake, a third the loss behaviour, and a third the migration — which is a good illustration that QUIC's win is several modest improvements compounding rather than one large one.

10. When TO Use This

  • When a measurable share of your users are on lossy or high-RTT networks. Mobile, international, congested Wi-Fi. This is the case QUIC was built for and the only one where the benefit is reliably large.

  • When clients reconnect frequently. Mobile apps backgrounding and foregrounding, users switching networks, short sessions. 0-RTT resumption and connection migration both pay off per reconnection, so high reconnect rates multiply the benefit.

  • When time-to-first-byte is the product metric. Search, chat, streaming interfaces — anywhere the user is waiting on the first response rather than on total transfer.

  • When you control the edge and can measure per-cohort. QUIC is an edge-termination technology in practice; if you can't segment your latency metrics by network type and protocol version, you can't justify or validate it.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Not on backend or backbone paths. Loss is negligible there, so per-stream recovery buys nothing, while you pay 2–3× the CPU per byte and give up mature TCP tooling. Terminate QUIC at the edge and speak HTTP/2 over TCP inland — that's what mature deployments do.

  • Not without a monitored TCP fallback. UDP on port 443 is blocked in enough enterprise and mobile networks that some users will never negotiate h3. The dangerous version of this isn't failure, it's silent success: everyone falls back, everything works, and you've paid the operational cost for a benefit that never activated.

  • Not with a 4-tuple-hashing L4 balancer in front. Connection migration and NAT rebinding will send packets to a backend with no state for that connection ID. The symptom is errors concentrated in users switching networks, which looks exactly like client flakiness. Fix the routing tier before enabling QUIC, not after.

  • Not with 0-RTT enabled indiscriminately. 0-RTT data has no replay protection, so it must be restricted to idempotent, non-state-changing requests. Treating it as a global speed switch turns a performance feature into a correctness bug.

  • Not as a substitute for shortening the path. Edge termination usually delivers a larger and cheaper win than a protocol change, and the two compound. If you haven't done the placement work, do that first.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "QUIC is faster because UDP is lighter than TCP."

✅ Reality: QUIC re-implements reliability, ordering and congestion control, so it is not lighter — it costs more CPU per byte than TCP, because that work happens in userspace without the kernel's offloads. UDP was chosen for middlebox traversal, not for weight. The gains come from the fused 1-RTT handshake, per-stream recovery, and connection migration.

❌ Misconception: "QUIC eliminates head-of-line blocking."

✅ Reality: It eliminates the connection-wide form. A stream still promises ordered delivery of its own bytes, so a loss inside one large response still stalls that response. QPACK also has to work carefully to avoid reintroducing blocking at the header-compression layer. The guarantee moved from per-connection to per-stream.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I read QUIC's userspace implementation as a temporary state — something that would migrate into kernels once it settled. It's the opposite: userspace is the feature. TCP's improvements are gated on kernel and middlebox upgrade cycles measured in years, which is why TCP Fast Open never landed broadly despite being standardised. QUIC's ability to ship a new congestion controller inside a browser release is the durable advantage, and it explains why the encrypted transport header exists — to stop middleboxes ossifying it the way they ossified TCP.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Saying "QUIC is UDP-based so it's faster". The immediate follow-up is "but it re-implements everything TCP does, so where does the speed come from?" and the answer has to be the 1-RTT fused handshake, per-stream recovery and migration. Leading with UDP invites the trap.

Not knowing why UDP specifically. The answer is middlebox traversal and userspace deployability, not performance. Getting this right is one of the most reliable depth signals on this topic, because it reframes the whole protocol as a deployment strategy.

Claiming HTTP/3 percentages without conditions. The benefit is conditional on loss and RTT. "Faster on lossy mobile paths, roughly neutral on a clean fixed line, and I'd measure our own cohorts before committing" is defensible; a bare percentage is not.

Ignoring the CPU cost. It's the most common operational surprise in a rollout and the thing an infrastructure reviewer will probe. Volunteering it — and the offloads that narrow it — signals you've deployed this rather than read about it.

Forgetting the fallback path. Any client-facing QUIC design needs Alt-Svc, a TCP fallback, and a metric for how often the fallback is used. An answer that ends at "we enable HTTP/3" has skipped the part most likely to bite.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Handshake, new connection 1 RTT Transport + TLS 1.3 fused, versus 2 RTT for TCP+TLS 1.3 RFC 9000 §7, RFC 9001
Handshake, resumed 0 RTT Application data in the first flight; no replay protection RFC 9001 §4.6
ALPN token h3 Negotiated in TLS; Alt-Svc is the discovery mechanism RFC 9114 §3.2
Connection identity Connection ID, 0–160 bits Not the 4-tuple — this is what enables migration RFC 9000 §5.1
Packet numbers Monotonic, never reused Removes TCP's retransmission ambiguity in RTT sampling RFC 9000 §12.3
Encryption Mandatory; payload + most of the header No unencrypted QUIC exists; ossification resistance by design RFC 9001
CPU cost versus TCP ~2–3× per byte early on, narrowing Userspace processing without kernel offloads; UDP GSO/GRO help Vendor deployment reports
Loss regime where it wins Above roughly 2% Below that, close to neutral against HTTP/2 Cloudflare HTTP/3 vs HTTP/2

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Halves handshake cost and confines stalls to one stream; no benefit at all on a clean, low-RTT path
💰 Cost Userspace packet processing raises edge CPU per gigabit — a real fleet-sizing line item against a tail-latency benefit
🔒 Security / visibility Encryption is mandatory and covers most of the transport header, which resists ossification and simultaneously blinds your capture tooling
📈 Scale Connection-ID routing must replace 4-tuple hashing at the LB, and UDP receive buffers must be raised; both are prerequisites, not tuning
🔧 Ops complexity Two protocol paths to operate and debug, a fallback to monitor, and Alt-Svc propagation delay bounding both rollout and rollback
🐛 Debuggability The largest single loss in this folder: tcpdump-based loss analysis stops working. qlog and QUIC-aware tooling are not optional extras

16. Real World Usage

QUIC began as Google's response to a measurement, not a theory. SPDY and HTTP/2 improved page loads on good networks and underdelivered on lossy mobile ones, and the diagnosis was TCP's connection-wide stall. Google deployed gQUIC across Chrome and its own services from 2013, gathered years of production data, and brought the result to the IETF — where it was substantially redesigned into RFC 9000 in 2021. The two-stage history is worth knowing, because "QUIC" sometimes still means the incompatible Google variant in older material.

CDNs are where it actually runs. Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai and the major cloud front-ends terminate HTTP/3 at the edge and speak HTTP/2 over TCP to origin — the split-transport topology from the Tier 4 answer, deployed at scale. Very few organisations run QUIC to origin, and that's a deliberate choice rather than an adoption lag.

Connection migration is the feature mobile teams notice. A user walking out of a building switches from Wi-Fi to cellular and their IP changes; TCP connections die and every in-flight request restarts, while QUIC continues on the same connection ID after path validation. For an app doing a long upload or holding a live stream, that's the difference between a visible failure and nothing at all.

17. Acronym Decoder

  • QUIC — originally an acronym for "Quick UDP Internet Connections", now formally just a name. RFC 9000 treats it as a proper noun, and the expansion teaches nothing about the mechanism, so don't decode it in a discussion.

  • ALPN — Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation. The TLS extension in which the client offers protocol tokens and the server picks; h3 selects HTTP/3, h2 HTTP/2. It's why version selection costs no extra round trip.

  • Alt-Svc — Alternative Services, RFC 7838. A response header telling the client "this origin is also available at h3 on this port for ma seconds". It's the discovery mechanism, and because the client acts on it at the next connection, its ma value bounds both rollout and rollback speed.

  • QPACK — QUIC-friendly header compression, RFC 9204. HPACK's dynamic table assumes total ordering across streams, which QUIC removes; QPACK re-does it with separate instruction streams so headers don't reintroduce blocking.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

  • 50-http2-remaining-flaw.md — the problem QUIC was built to solve; this note is unmotivated without it

  • ../03-tcp-udp/29-when-udp-is-right.md — why UDP is a substrate here rather than a semantic choice

  • ../03-tcp-udp/20-three-way-handshake.md — the 2-RTT setup cost QUIC halves

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 52-quic-connection-migration.md — the connection-ID mechanism in detail

  • 53-http3-semantics-over-quic.md — what HTTP/3 adds on top, and what it deliberately leaves unchanged

  • 54-when-each-version-matters.md — the decision framework that decides whether any of this is worth it for you

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • HTTP/2 over TCP — the right default on clean paths, cheaper in CPU, far easier to debug

  • Edge termination alone — often a bigger and cheaper win than the protocol change; do it first, and they compound

  • WebTransport — QUIC's datagram and stream API exposed to browsers, for cases where HTTP semantics aren't wanted at all

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Alt-Svc and ALPN — discovery and selection, and the lever for rollout and rollback

  • TLS 1.3 — not layered on but fused in; there is no QUIC without it

  • Anycast edge PoPs — QUIC's benefits and edge placement compound, which is why they're deployed together

19. System Design Application

Skipped — the architect-level rollout treatment is discharged by the Section 3 Tier 4 follow-up (staged deployment, topology, and the three failure modes). The cross-version design story with capacity and SLOs is owned by 54-when-each-version-matters.md for the whole arc, and the tail-latency monitoring story by 50-http2-remaining-flaw.md, rather than being repeated here.

notes.title: Connection Migration in QUIC

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
If the client's address just changed, how does the server know it's the same client and not an attacker?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
What does supporting migration cost you in infrastructure?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Connection migration — RFC 9000 §9: Connection Migration

  • Connection IDs — RFC 9000 §5.1: Connection ID

  • Path validation — RFC 9000 §8.2: Path Validation

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What identifies a QUIC connection? A connection ID in the packet header — not the 4-tuple.
What must happen before the new path is used fully? Path validation: PATH_CHALLENGE / PATH_RESPONSE, to prove reachability.
What does this require of your load balancer? Routing by connection ID, not by 4-tuple hash. Otherwise migration breaks.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A TCP connection is its four-tuple, so when a phone moves from Wi-Fi to cellular and its IP changes, the connection is dead and every in-flight request restarts after a fresh handshake. QUIC identifies a connection by a connection ID carried in the packet header instead, so the same connection continues from the new address — after a challenge-response that proves the new path is genuinely reachable. For a mobile user mid-upload or mid-stream, that's the difference between a visible failure and nothing at all. The catch is that your load balancer must route by that ID.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

If the client's address just changed, how does the server know it's the same client and not an attacker?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know migration is authenticated and rate-limited, rather than a trust-the-header mechanism.

Two mechanisms, and both are necessary. First, packets are authenticated: QUIC packets are protected with keys established during the handshake, so an attacker who observes a connection ID cannot produce valid packets for it. Simply spoofing an ID gets you nothing, because the payload won't authenticate. That alone establishes identity.

What it doesn't establish is reachability, and that's the second mechanism. An attacker could replay a genuine packet with a forged source address to point the server's traffic at a victim — an amplification attack. So on seeing a new address the server sends PATH_CHALLENGE containing random data and waits for a PATH_RESPONSE echoing it back, which only something actually at that address can produce. Until validation completes the server limits how much it will send on the new path, capping amplification. There's a privacy dimension too: connection IDs are rotated, with each endpoint issuing spare IDs in advance via NEW_CONNECTION_ID, so an on-path observer can't trivially link a user's activity across networks by watching a constant identifier.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

What does supporting migration cost you in infrastructure?

📍 Seen in the wild: the question that decides whether an HTTP/3 rollout works or produces mystifying errors for mobile users.

It costs you your load-balancing model. Standard L4 balancers hash the 4-tuple to pick a backend, which is exactly the thing that just changed — so a migrated client's packets hash differently and land on a backend holding no state for that connection ID, which drops them. The symptom is brutal to diagnose because it's narrow and intermittent: errors concentrated in users switching networks, invisible in aggregate, and indistinguishable from client flakiness unless you're segmenting by that event. The fix is that every device in the path must route by connection ID, which means either a QUIC-aware balancer or the encoding trick real deployments use — servers issue connection IDs with routing information embedded in them, so a stateless balancer can extract the destination from the ID without holding connection state.

The second cost is server-side state lifetime. Because a connection survives address changes, it can persist across network transitions for far longer than a TCP connection would, so per-connection memory is held longer and connection counts drift upward. You need explicit idle timeouts and connection-age limits, and you need to size for the longer-lived population. Both costs are real, and both are prerequisites rather than tuning: enabling QUIC behind a 4-tuple-hashing balancer breaks migration for exactly the mobile users the feature exists to help, which is the worst possible failure distribution.

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The mechanism turns on one substitution. TCP's connection identity is (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port), so any change to any element destroys it. QUIC's identity is the destination connection ID in the packet header, which the peer chose and which does not change when the network path does. The 4-tuple becomes merely the current path — a routing detail, not an identity.

What migration saves on a network switch, 60ms RTT: TCP + TLS 1.3: connection dies → 1 RTT (TCP) + 1 RTT (TLS) = 120ms, plus every in-flight request restarted from scratch. QUIC: 1 RTT of path validation, overlapping continued use of the old path where available → ~0ms user-visible, no requests lost. The saving isn't primarily the 120ms — it's not losing the in-flight work, which for an upload or a live stream is the whole difference.

Two details worth carrying. Each endpoint issues spare connection IDs in advance via NEW_CONNECTION_ID, so the client can switch to a fresh, unused ID when it migrates — which is what stops a passive observer from linking a user across networks by a constant identifier. And migration is client-initiated only: servers may not migrate, because a server changing address would be indistinguishable from an attack.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't enable QUIC behind a 4-tuple-hashing L4 balancer. Migration will break precisely for the mobile users it's meant to help, and the errors will look like client flakiness. Connection-ID routing is a prerequisite for the rollout, not an optimisation to add afterwards.

  • Don't assume migration means connections never end. Idle timeouts still apply, NAT rebinding still triggers validation, and a client that backgrounds for long enough will still reconnect. Migration removes a class of interruption; it doesn't make connections eternal.

  • Don't count on it for server-side failover. Migration is client-initiated by design. If your backend goes away, the connection dies exactly as a TCP one would — this is not a high-availability mechanism.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Connection migration means QUIC connections survive anything."

✅ Reality: It survives client address changes, which is one specific and common event. Idle timeouts, server restarts and explicit closes all still terminate the connection, and each migration costs a path-validation round trip with limited sending until it completes.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I filed migration as a minor convenience next to per-stream loss recovery. For mobile products it's often the more visible feature — a user walking out of a building mid-upload sees the upload continue rather than fail, and that's a bug report that stops arriving. It's also the feature with the sharpest infrastructure prerequisite, which makes it the one most likely to be broken by an otherwise-correct rollout.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)
