notes.title: HTTP/3 — HTTP Semantics over QUIC

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
If the semantics are identical, what is HTTP/3 actually specifying?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
Two protocol paths at the edge. How do clients choose, and what does that cost you operationally?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • HTTP/3 — RFC 9114: HTTP/3

  • Connection setup and the h3 ALPN token — RFC 9114 §3.2

  • Header compression for out-of-order streams — RFC 9204: QPACK

  • The semantics that didn't change — RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What changed from HTTP/2 to HTTP/3? The transport, the header compression, and connection-level flow control. Not the semantics.
Why QPACK instead of HPACK? HPACK assumes total ordering across streams; QUIC removes it.
What did QUIC absorb from HTTP/2? Streams, flow control and multiplexing moved down into the transport.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

HTTP/3 is HTTP's same semantics — same methods, same status codes, same headers — mapped onto QUIC instead of TCP. The interesting part is what HTTP/3 stopped doing: QUIC already provides streams, multiplexing and flow control, so HTTP/3 deletes HTTP/2's own versions of all three and just uses the transport's. What it had to replace is header compression, because HPACK assumes headers arrive in order and QUIC's whole point is that they don't. That's QPACK, and its existence is the clearest sign the change ran deeper than swapping transports.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

If the semantics are identical, what is HTTP/3 actually specifying?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can articulate the layering shift — that HTTP/3 is smaller than HTTP/2, not bigger.

A mapping, and a notably thin one. RFC 9114 says how HTTP requests and responses map onto QUIC streams: each request/response exchange gets its own client-initiated bidirectional stream, so the "stream" concept HTTP/2 invented at the application layer is now just the transport's stream. Framing is simpler too — HTTP/3 has its own small set of frames (HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS) but no WINDOW_UPDATE, no RST_STREAM, no PRIORITY, because QUIC provides flow control, stream reset and (via a separate header-based scheme) prioritisation directly.

So the mental model is that capabilities moved down a layer. HTTP/2 built multiplexing on top of a transport that couldn't do it; QUIC does it natively, so HTTP/3 stops re-implementing it. The one thing HTTP/3 could not delegate is header compression, because compression is inherently about state shared across messages and QUIC has no opinion on message boundaries. HPACK's dynamic table assumes total ordering — block N may reference an entry added by block N−1 — which is exactly the assumption QUIC breaks. QPACK re-does it with separate unidirectional encoder and decoder streams and explicit handling for blocked streams, so a header block that references a not-yet-received table entry stalls only itself.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Two protocol paths at the edge. How do clients choose, and what does that cost you operationally?

📍 Seen in the wild: the deployment question, and the one where Alt-Svc's propagation delay surprises people.

Clients discover HTTP/3 through Alt-Svc. A server responds over HTTP/2 with Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400, meaning "this origin is also reachable via h3 on port 443, and you may cache that fact for 86400 seconds". The client does not switch mid-connection — it uses the alternative on its next connection to the origin. So the first visit is always over TCP, and HTTP/3 begins on a subsequent one. That single behaviour has two consequences people miss: rollout is gradual by construction, and rollback is bounded by the ma you advertised, because clients keep using h3 until the cached entry expires. Keep ma short until you're confident, or a bad HTTP/3 day lasts as long as you told clients it would.

The operational cost is that you now run and debug two paths permanently. UDP 443 must be open through every firewall and load balancer, and the LB must route by connection ID rather than 4-tuple or migration breaks. Edge CPU per byte rises because QUIC processes packets in userspace. Your tcpdump-based diagnosis stops working, since QUIC encrypts most of its transport header — you need qlog and QUIC-aware tooling and people who can read them. And every incident now starts with "which protocol was this user on?", which means logging the negotiated version per request is not optional instrumentation. The most dangerous failure is the quiet one: a firewall blocks UDP, clients fall back silently, everything works, and the investment returns nothing for that population. Alert on h3 share by region and ASN.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Concern HTTP/2 HTTP/3 Where it lives now
Streams Defined by HTTP/2 framing Provided by QUIC Transport
Multiplexing HTTP/2 framing layer QUIC Transport
Flow control Per-stream + per-connection WINDOW_UPDATE QUIC's own Transport
Stream reset RST_STREAM frame QUIC RESET_STREAM Transport
Header compression HPACK (order-dependent) QPACK Application — the one thing that couldn't move
Encryption Optional in spec, mandatory in browsers Mandatory, part of the transport Transport
Semantics RFC 9110 RFC 9110 Unchanged — the point
ALPN token h2 h3 Negotiated in TLS

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The diagram is the answer to "what is HTTP/3": the middle layer got thinner because the layer below got thicker. HTTP/2's framing layer carries streams, multiplexing, flow control and compression; HTTP/3's carries a request-to-stream mapping and QPACK, because QUIC absorbed the rest. TLS also moved — layered on TCP in the HTTP/2 stack, fused into QUIC in the HTTP/3 one, which is why the handshake collapses from 2 RTT to 1.

QPACK's design is worth one concrete beat, because it's the thing that had to be invented. It runs two extra unidirectional QUIC streams — an encoder stream carrying table insertions and a decoder stream carrying acknowledgements — separate from the request streams. A header block may reference a dynamic-table entry, and if that entry's insertion hasn't arrived yet the decoder blocks that stream only while the rest proceed. The encoder can also choose to avoid risky references entirely, trading compression ratio for zero blocking:

The QPACK dial. Aggressive dynamic-table references → better compression, some risk of per-stream blocking. Conservative references → slightly larger headers, no blocking. SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS bounds how many streams may be blocked at once; setting it to 0 disables the risk entirely at a modest compression cost.

This is the general shape of the HTTP/2-to-HTTP/3 change: nothing about what HTTP means moved, and everything about how state is shared across concurrent messages had to be reconsidered.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't expect application changes to be needed — or to help. Semantics are identical, so your handlers, status codes and caching logic are untouched. Conversely, nothing you do at the application layer produces HTTP/3's benefit; it's an edge and transport concern entirely.

  • Don't advertise Alt-Svc with a long ma during rollout. It bounds your rollback speed: clients keep using h3 until the cached entry expires, so a long ma means a long bad day. Start short and raise it once stable.

  • Don't deploy without logging the negotiated protocol version per request. Without it you cannot detect silent fallback, cannot segment latency by version, and cannot answer the first question of any incident. It's the cheapest instrumentation in the rollout and the one most often skipped.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "HTTP/3 is a big new version of HTTP."

✅ Reality: It's the smallest of the three specifications in terms of what it defines, because QUIC absorbed streams, multiplexing and flow control. The semantics are byte-for-byte the same RFC 9110 that HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 use. Nearly all of what people call "HTTP/3" is actually QUIC.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I assumed HTTP/3 was HTTP/2's framing layer running over QUIC, with the transport swapped underneath. It's more of a deletion: HTTP/3 removes HTTP/2's stream, flow-control and reset machinery because QUIC already has it, and the only thing it had to genuinely rebuild was header compression. Realising the layer got thinner rather than thicker is what made the QPACK question — "why couldn't they just keep HPACK?" — answerable.

📚 Reference Links

  • Measured comparison under varying loss — Comparing HTTP/3 vs. HTTP/2 Performance

  • What each version changed — MDN: Evolution of HTTP

  • HTTP/2's own scope statement — RFC 9113 §1: Introduction

  • HTTP/3's — RFC 9114 §1: Introduction

  • Bonus — the performance treatment of the arc: High Performance Browser Networking: HTTP/2

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Where is HTTP/2's gain largest? Many concurrent requests, one origin, high RTT. It deletes the ÷ 6 serialisation term.
Where is HTTP/2's gain ~zero? One request at a time; low RTT; a single large download.
Where is HTTP/3's gain largest? Lossy paths (>~2%), high reconnect rates, mobile. It's a tail improvement.
Where is HTTP/3's gain ~zero or negative? Clean fixed-line paths, backend/backbone hops — and it costs 2–3× CPU per byte.
The metric that decides it? p99/p50 ratio segmented by network type — not aggregate latency.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

The versions fix three different bottlenecks, so the right one depends on which one you have. HTTP/2 removes request serialisation, so it wins with many concurrent requests to one origin over a high-RTT path and does roughly nothing for a single large download on a fast link. HTTP/3 removes the connection-wide stall on packet loss, so it wins on lossy mobile paths and does roughly nothing on a clean fixed line — while costing two to three times the CPU per byte. The decision isn't which version is newest; it's which bottleneck your p99 actually has.

4. Quick Comparison Table — the centrepiece

The bottleneck each version removes

Version Bottleneck it removes Gain is large when Gain is ~zero when What it costs
HTTP/1.1 — (the baseline) — — Serialisation, 6 handshakes, 6 cold windows
HTTP/2 Request serialisation (app-layer blocking) Many concurrent requests to one origin; high RTT; large repetitive headers One request at a time; low RTT; one big download Connection-wide stall under loss; L4 balancing breaks; binary wire
HTTP/3 Connection-wide stall under loss; 1 of 2 setup RTTs Loss >~2%; high reconnect rate; mobile and long international paths Clean low-loss paths; backend hops ~2–3× CPU per byte; UDP through infra; two paths to operate

By workload — the version this table exists to give you

Workload Pick Why Expected gain
Browser page, 100+ assets, 150ms+ RTT HTTP/2, then HTTP/3 Deletes RTT × ceil(assets÷6); ~4× on the trace in item 46 Large
Same page, all users on a 10ms LAN HTTP/2, but don't expect much Serialisation term is already tiny Small
Mobile app, cellular, frequent reconnects HTTP/3 Per-stream recovery + 0-RTT resumption + migration, all compounding Large, in the tail
Single large file download Any — version is irrelevant One stream; bounded by congestion window and bandwidth ~Zero
LLM token streaming to consumers HTTP/3 at the edge Sparse writes miss fast retransmit and hit the 1s RTO floor Large, in the tail
gRPC between services, same region HTTP/2 (mandatory for gRPC) Multiplexing collapses connection count; loss negligible Large operationally
gRPC across regions or over VPN HTTP/2, but watch p99 Correlated stalls across unrelated RPCs on the shared connection Mixed — measure
Service mesh, sidecar to sidecar HTTP/2 One connection per proxy pair; removes port-exhaustion class Large operationally
Edge → origin backhaul over a backbone HTTP/2 over TCP Loss negligible, so HTTP/3 buys nothing and costs CPU ~Zero, negative on cost
Webhook receiver / cron client / CLI HTTP/1.1 No concurrency to multiplex; inspectable with tcpdump and nc ~Zero
Any client behind a UDP-blocking firewall HTTP/2, with h3 offered Fallback will carry it anyway — monitor the ratio ~Zero until UDP works

The gains that are commonly overclaimed

Claim Reality
"HTTP/2 is faster because binary parses faster" Parsing was never the bottleneck. The gain is multiplexing plus one warm connection
"HTTP/2 fixed head-of-line blocking" App-layer only. Transport-layer got worse — one connection, one blast radius
"HTTP/3 is X% faster" Conditional on loss and RTT. Near-neutral on a clean path; measure your own cohorts
"QUIC is faster because UDP is lighter" QUIC costs more CPU per byte. UDP was chosen for middlebox traversal
"Newer is better for everything" On backbone hops HTTP/3 is a pure cost. Version choice is per-hop, not per-company

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Name a case where upgrading from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2 buys you nothing.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can articulate the mechanism well enough to find its boundary, rather than defaulting to "newer is better".

A single large file download. HTTP/2's gain is the removal of request serialisation — it deletes the RTT × ceil(assets ÷ 6) term from load time. One request has nothing to serialise, so there is nothing to delete; the transfer is bounded by the congestion window and available bandwidth, both of which are properties of TCP and identical under either version. You'll measure noise.

The same reasoning gives you the other zero-gain cases, and being able to generate them rather than recite them is the point. A client that makes one request at a time — a cron job, a webhook receiver — has no concurrency to multiplex. A page served over a 5ms LAN has a serialisation term of milliseconds, so removing it is unmeasurable. And a page already reduced to eight requests through concatenation gets far less than a page with 120. Conversely the maximum-gain case is the mirror image: many small requests, one origin, high RTT — which is exactly the mobile page load the protocol was designed against.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Your CTO asks why you haven't enabled HTTP/3. Make the case for not doing it.

📍 Seen in the wild: the reversal, which is a much better test than the advocacy version.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can decline a fashionable upgrade with evidence, which is a more useful architect skill than championing one.

Start with what the benefit is and where it lands: HTTP/3's advantage is per-stream loss recovery and a halved handshake, so it improves the tail for users on lossy or high-RTT paths. If our traffic is predominantly desktop clients on fixed lines — and the measurement to bring is p99/p50 ratio segmented by network type — then those cohorts show a ratio close to the fixed-line baseline, retransmission counters at the edge are near zero, and there is no tail for HTTP/3 to improve. The honest expected gain is within noise.

Against that, the costs are concrete and immediate. Edge CPU per byte rises roughly two to three-fold because packet processing moves from the kernel into userspace without offloads, so the fleet is sized differently. UDP must traverse load balancers and firewalls, which may mean a different LB product. We would operate and debug two protocol paths permanently, and QUIC's encrypted transport headers mean our existing tcpdump-based loss diagnosis stops working — we'd need qlog tooling and the skills to use it. The recommendation is therefore: build the per-cohort measurement now, because we need it either way; revisit when mobile or international traffic grows past a threshold we set in advance; and in the meantime spend the same effort on edge placement, which reduces RTT for everyone and is a larger, cheaper win. That's a defensible "no" with a trigger for revisiting, which is different from — and better than — a reflexive one.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

A quarter of your traffic goes to a UDP-blocking enterprise network. What breaks, and how do you know?

📍 Seen in the wild: the failure mode that costs money quietly, and the reason Alt-Svc share is a metric rather than a curiosity.

Nothing breaks — that's precisely the problem. Those clients attempt QUIC, fail to establish, and fall back to HTTP/2 over TCP. Every request succeeds, no errors are logged, no alert fires. What has run out is not a resource but the return on the investment: you are paying for a QUIC-capable edge fleet, the larger CPU footprint, the dual-path operational burden and the QUIC tooling, and a quarter of your users receive none of the benefit. Worse, that quarter may be disproportionately the enterprise customers with the strictest latency expectations.

It presents as an absence rather than a signal, which is why it has to be instrumented deliberately: log the negotiated protocol version per request and chart the h3 share segmented by ASN, region and customer tier. A healthy rollout shows h3 share climbing toward the fraction of clients that support it and staying there; a blocked-UDP population shows a share that plateaus low and correlates with specific networks. The secondary signal is Alt-Svc advertisement versus uptake — you're advertising to everyone and only some are taking it. The remediation isn't technical so much as commercial: identify the affected customers, and either work with their network teams to open UDP 443 or accept and document that they're on the HTTP/2 path. Either way the decision needs the number, and without the per-cohort logging you will never have it.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the protocol strategy for a product serving browsers, mobile apps, and internal services. One answer per hop.

🎯 Really testing: whether you assign versions per hop based on that hop's bottleneck, or reach for a single company-wide answer.

The highest-stakes framing is that version choice is a property of a hop, not of an organisation, because each hop has a different bottleneck. Say that first; it reframes the question and it's the thing most answers get wrong by picking one version and applying it everywhere.

Hop by hop. Browser to edge: HTTP/3 offered via Alt-Svc with HTTP/2 as the monitored fallback — browsers make many concurrent requests over variable-quality paths, which is both versions' best case. Mobile app to edge: HTTP/3 preferred, and this is where it earns most, because reconnect rate is high so 0-RTT resumption and connection migration compound with the loss behaviour. Edge to origin over the backbone: HTTP/2 over TCP, deliberately — loss is negligible so per-stream recovery buys nothing, and TCP is cheaper in CPU and far easier to debug. Service to service inside a region: HTTP/2, and mandatory where gRPC is involved; the win here is operational rather than latency — one connection per pair instead of a pool, which removes the port-exhaustion class of failure. Sidecar to sidecar in a mesh: HTTP/2, upgraded transparently by the proxies even where applications speak 1.1. Webhooks out to third parties: HTTP/1.1, because you don't control the receiver and inspectability matters more than concurrency you don't have.

Two constraints thread through all of it. Every hop terminating HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 needs an L7 balancer, because multiplexing is unbalanceable at L4 — one connection carrying a hundred requests is an indivisible unit to a connection-level device. And every backend needs connection-age recycling, or long-lived multiplexed connections pin their streams to whichever pod they landed on and newly scaled instances receive no traffic.

The failure I'd monitor first is request-distribution skew across backends, ahead of any latency metric. It's the quiet one: connections established before a scale-out keep serving, new pods idle, aggregate latency creeps up, every health check passes and nothing errors. A healthy L7 tier holds the busiest-to-quietest backend ratio near 1; a drift past 3 means connections have pinned and the multiplexing you adopted for efficiency has become a load-balancing bug.

📖 DEPTH BLOCK

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Conditional section, satisfied by the decision flowchart in Section 4 — the mechanisms themselves are owned by items 46, 48, 50 and 51 and are not repeated here. What this note adds is the arithmetic that decides between them:

HTTP/1.1 → HTTP/2 gain ≈ the serialisation term you delete: RTT × ceil(assets ÷ 6). 120 assets at 200ms → 4000ms deleted. 8 assets at 20ms → 40ms deleted, which is noise. The gain scales with assets × RTT. Both must be large.

HTTP/2 → HTTP/3 gain ≈ the stalls you stop sharing, plus one handshake RTT. Expected stalls per page ≈ packets × loss_rate. At 300 packets and 2% loss that's ~6 stalls, each previously blocking all streams and now blocking one. The gain scales with loss_rate × concurrency, and shows up in p99, not p50. At 0.05% loss the term vanishes.

That pair of expressions is the note. Every row in Section 4's tables is one of them evaluated at a particular workload, and if you can reconstruct the two expressions you can generate the table rather than memorise it.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The observable is which percentile you are optimising, and the versions do not compete on the same one. HTTP/2's win shows up in median page load, because request serialisation affected every load equally. HTTP/3's win shows up almost entirely in p99 for a subset of users, because loss is intermittent and unevenly distributed. Teams that evaluate HTTP/3 against an aggregate mean conclude it does nothing — which is a true statement about the mean and a false conclusion about the protocol.

The second reason it matters is cost attribution. HTTP/3 raises edge CPU per gigabit, which is a line item someone will notice, and it must be justified against a benefit measured in a cohort. "Our cellular p99 dropped from 2.4s to 1.6s and cellular is 31% of sessions" is an argument. "HTTP/3 is faster" is not, and will lose to a finance question.

9. Worked Decision Scenarios

Per the table/playbook override, the trace is replaced by decision walkthroughs: situation → the checks in order → the answer → the one-sentence defence.

Scenario 1 — "Our React SPA is slow for users in Singapore; we're on HTTP/1.1." Checks: how many requests per page load? (94) What's the RTT? (210ms from your Frankfurt origin) Any domain sharding in place? (yes, three subdomains) → HTTP/2, plus remove the sharding, plus an APAC edge. Defence: the load time contains 210ms × ceil(94÷6) ≈ 3.4s of pure serialisation, HTTP/2 deletes that term entirely, and the sharding must go or it splits the single connection that makes it work.

Scenario 2 — "Should we move our internal gRPC mesh to HTTP/3?" Checks: what's the loss rate between pods? (effectively zero) Is p99 diverging from p50? (no) What's the CPU headroom on the sidecars? (tight) → No. Stay on HTTP/2. Defence: HTTP/3's benefit is per-stream recovery under loss, there is no loss on this path, and we would pay 2–3× packet-processing CPU on sidecars that are already the mesh's main overhead.

Scenario 3 — "Our LLM chat streams stutter for some users but our latency dashboard is green." Checks: is the dashboard showing means or the inter-token gap distribution? (means) Is proxy_buffering off on the SSE path? (not verified) Do the affected users cluster by network type? (unknown — not segmented) → Rule out the buffering proxy first, then segment p99 by network type; if it's transport, HTTP/3 at the edge. Defence: a buffering proxy and transport head-of-line blocking produce the same symptom, one costs a config line to test and the other is a platform project, so check the cheap one first.

Scenario 4 — "We're building a webhook sender to thousands of customer endpoints." Checks: how many requests per endpoint? (a handful, bursty) Do you control the receivers? (no) Does inspectability matter when a customer says delivery failed? (very much) → HTTP/1.1 with a connection pool. Defence: there's no per-endpoint concurrency to multiplex, we don't control the receivers so we can't rely on HTTP/2 support, and being able to reproduce a customer's failure with curl -v is worth more here than any protocol gain.

Scenario 5 — "Marketing wants us to advertise HTTP/3 support. Two-week deadline." Checks: do we have per-cohort latency measurement? (no) Does our LB route by connection ID? (no, 4-tuple) Is UDP 443 open through the edge? (unknown) → Not in two weeks. Sequence it: measurement first, then LB routing, then one PoP behind Alt-Svc with a short ma. Defence: enabling QUIC behind a 4-tuple-hashing balancer breaks connection migration for exactly the mobile users it's meant to help, and without per-cohort measurement we couldn't tell whether it worked.

10. When TO Use This

This note is the decision procedure, so this section is when to run it:

  • When choosing the protocol for a new hop. Version is a per-hop decision, and the two expressions in Section 6 answer it in about a minute.

  • When someone proposes an upgrade without a number. The table's last column — expected gain — is the question to ask, and it's often "~zero".

  • When p99 and p50 have diverged and you don't know why. The version arc supplies three candidate mechanisms and the measurement that separates them.

  • When justifying infrastructure spend. Edge CPU for HTTP/3 has to be argued against a cohort-specific benefit, and this is where that argument gets assembled.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't apply one version company-wide. The backbone hop and the mobile last mile have opposite bottlenecks; a single answer is wrong for at least one of them, and usually pays cost where there's no benefit.

  • Don't upgrade without unwinding the previous era's workarounds. Domain sharding, concatenation and sprites were HTTP/1.1 mitigations, and sharding actively harms HTTP/2. Upgrading without removing them measures as failure and gets blamed on the protocol.

  • Don't evaluate against aggregate averages. HTTP/3's entire benefit lives in a cohort's tail. An aggregate mean is structurally incapable of showing it, and will produce a confident wrong conclusion in either direction.

  • Don't treat this table as durable. The 2% crossover, the CPU ratio and the fallback rates all move as implementations and networks improve. The two expressions in Section 6 are the durable part; the rows are today's evaluation of them.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Newer versions are faster, so upgrade everywhere."

✅ Reality: Each version removes a specific bottleneck. On a hop that doesn't have that bottleneck you get no benefit and pay the cost — HTTP/3 on a backbone link is pure CPU overhead for zero latency gain. Version choice is per-hop.

❌ Misconception: "We tried HTTP/2 and saw no improvement, so it's overhyped."

✅ Reality: Almost always one of three things — measured on a low-RTT path where the serialisation term was already tiny, measured on a workload with little concurrency, or measured with domain sharding still in place splitting the connection. The protocol's gain is assets × RTT; if either factor is small, so is the gain.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I treated the version arc as a straight upgrade path where each release strictly dominated the last. It isn't — HTTP/2 made transport-layer blocking worse than six connections did, and HTTP/3 costs more CPU than TCP. Each step is a trade that pays off under specific conditions, and knowing the conditions is the actual skill. That reframing is also what makes the "argue against HTTP/3" question answerable instead of uncomfortable.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

This section carries unusual weight for table topics — it's where confidently wrong one-word answers live.

Answering "HTTP/3, it's the newest". The reflex answer, and it fails the moment you're asked about the backbone hop or the webhook sender. Lead with "which hop?" instead; that single question reframes you as someone who has deployed this.

Quoting a performance percentage with no conditions. "HTTP/3 is 30% faster" invites "under what loss rate, and on which cohort?" and there's no recovery. Attach the condition to the claim.

Not being able to name a zero-gain case. If every case in your answer is a win, you're describing marketing rather than engineering. A single large download over HTTP/2 is the cleanest example and it's worth having ready.

Forgetting that HTTP/2 made something worse. Multiplexing concentrated the blast radius of packet loss. Volunteering the regression is the strongest single signal available on this topic, because it demonstrates you understand the trade rather than the headline.

Skipping the operational cost. UDP through firewalls, connection-ID routing, edge CPU, dual-path debugging, Alt-Svc propagation. An answer that's purely about latency has ignored everything that actually makes the rollout hard.

Recommending an upgrade without a measurement plan. The senior move is naming the metric you'd check first — p99/p50 by network type — and saying what result would make you not proceed.

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency HTTP/2 buys median, HTTP/3 buys tail. They are not substitutes and shouldn't be evaluated with the same metric
💰 Cost HTTP/2 reduces handshake CPU by collapsing connections; HTTP/3 raises packet-processing CPU. The arc is not monotonically cheaper
🔒 Security / visibility Each version encrypts more and reveals less. HTTP/1.1 is readable, HTTP/2 needs a frame-aware tool, QUIC needs keys and qlog
📈 Scale Multiplexing collapses connection count and simultaneously breaks L4 balancing; every upgrade past 1.1 forces an L7 tier
🔧 Ops complexity Each version adds required infrastructure: L7 balancing for HTTP/2, UDP plus connection-ID routing plus a monitored fallback for HTTP/3
🐛 Debuggability Monotonically worse across the arc, and it's the cost most often left out of the comparison — worth pricing explicitly at 3am

16. Real World Usage

The "we upgraded and saw nothing" pattern is common enough to be diagnostic. It almost always resolves to domain sharding left in place after an HTTP/2 migration, splitting traffic across origins so no single connection accumulates a warm window or a populated HPACK table. The optimisation and the protocol are in direct conflict, and only one of them can be right at a time.

CDNs run split-transport topologies deliberately. Cloudflare, Fastly and the major cloud front-ends terminate HTTP/3 at the edge and speak HTTP/2 over TCP to origin. That isn't an adoption lag — it's the per-hop reasoning in this note, deployed: QUIC where the last mile is lossy, TCP where the backbone isn't.

Server push is the arc's cautionary tale. It shipped in HTTP/2 with a sound theoretical case and was abandoned because servers couldn't know what clients had cached, so it pushed bytes that were discarded. Chrome removed support in 2022 and 103 Early Hints replaced the idea. It's a good short answer to "name a protocol feature that looked good and wasn't", and a reminder that shipped standards are not the same as validated ones.

17. Acronym Decoder

  • ALPN — Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation. The TLS extension carrying the client's protocol list (h3, h2, http/1.1); the server picks one. Version selection therefore costs no extra round trip.

  • Alt-Svc — Alternative Services, RFC 7838. The response header advertising h3 availability. The client acts on it at its next connection, so the ma value bounds both rollout and rollback speed — a deployment lever, not just a header.

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

Typically as a challenge rather than a question: "we're on HTTP/1.1, should we upgrade?" or the sharper reversal, "argue against HTTP/3". What's being tested is whether you assign versions per hop from each hop's bottleneck, whether you can name a case where the newer version is worse, and whether you attach a measurement to the recommendation. The strongest shape is: here are the two expressions, here is the metric I'd check, here is the result that would make me not proceed.

Topology diagram

Note the deliberate version change at each boundary: HTTP/3 where the path is lossy, HTTP/2 over TCP where it isn't. A single company-wide version would be wrong on one side of the edge or the other.

Global, a third mobile Long-haul RTT and last-mile loss now dominate the tail for a large cohort Edge PoPs first (bigger, cheaper win), then HTTP/3 at the edge with a monitored fallback
Global, 10M+ users, strict SLOs Two protocol paths at every PoP, UDP capacity, QUIC CPU, tooling gap QUIC-capable edge fleet sized for ~2–3× packet CPU, qlog sampling, per-cohort SLOs, h3-share alerting

The money question is that HTTP/3 raises edge CPU per gigabit against a benefit confined to a cohort. The case has to be built as cohort size × latency improvement × business value, and if that product doesn't clear the fleet cost, not upgrading is the correct engineering answer.

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • At 10x: p99 diverges from p50 for one cohort while aggregate dashboards stay flat — the version decision becomes invisible to the metrics you have.

  • At 100x: multiplexed connections pin streams to backends, so scale-outs don't receive traffic and distribution skew grows silently behind passing health checks.

  • Operationally: a firewall blocks UDP for a customer segment, everything keeps working on the fallback, and the investment quietly returns nothing for a quarter of users.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • p99/p50 ratio by network type and negotiated HTTP version. The metric that makes every decision in this note verifiable. Alert on divergence between cohorts, not on absolute p99.

  • Negotiated-version share by region and ASN. Detects silent fallback, which is the failure mode with no other signal.

  • Backend request-distribution skew (busiest ÷ quietest). Catches stream pinning, which multiplexing causes and health checks never reveal.

  • Edge CPU per gigabit, segmented by protocol version. The capacity model that a protocol-mix shift will otherwise break without warning.

notes.title: gRPC's Dependence on HTTP/2 — and the Load-Balancing Problem

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
Why is gRPC tied to HTTP/2 specifically? Couldn't it run on HTTP/1.1?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
Your gRPC service scales from 3 pods to 30 and latency doesn't improve. Diagnose it.
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The four RPC types — gRPC: Core concepts

  • Official load-balancing guidance — gRPC Load Balancing

  • The streams gRPC maps onto — RFC 9113 §5: Streams and Multiplexing

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does an RPC map onto? One HTTP/2 stream. Bidirectional streaming = one stream carrying frames both ways.
Why does L4 balancing fail? It balances connections; one connection now carries hundreds of RPCs.
The three fixes? L7 balancer, client-side load balancing, or MAX_CONNECTION_AGE recycling.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

gRPC has no HTTP/1.1 mode — each RPC is an HTTP/2 stream, and its streaming call types are literally long-lived streams carrying frames in both directions. That gets you multiplexing, cancellation and flow control for free. It also gets you the load-balancing problem: an L4 balancer distributes connections, and one gRPC connection now carries hundreds of RPCs pinned to a single backend. Scale out and the new pods receive nothing, because no new connections are being made. You need an L7 balancer, client-side balancing, or forced connection recycling.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why is gRPC tied to HTTP/2 specifically? Couldn't it run on HTTP/1.1?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can map gRPC's features onto HTTP/2 mechanisms rather than treating the dependency as arbitrary.

Because three of gRPC's four call types have no HTTP/1.1 expression. Unary RPC maps fine onto a request/response pair. But server streaming needs the server to send many messages over time on one exchange, client streaming needs the client to do the same, and bidirectional streaming needs both at once on the same exchange — and HTTP/1.1 has one request body and one response body per connection slot, with no way to interleave. You could fake server streaming with chunked encoding, but client streaming and bidirectional have no analogue at all.

HTTP/2 supplies each of these directly. A stream is bidirectional by definition, so bidi streaming is one stream with DATA frames flowing both ways. Multiplexing means a thousand concurrent RPCs share one connection instead of needing a thousand. RST_STREAM gives per-RPC cancellation without disturbing the connection — which matters enormously for a system where deadline-driven cancellation is idiomatic. Per-stream flow control stops one large streaming RPC from starving the others. And trailers, which HTTP/2 supports properly, are how gRPC returns its status after the body, which is what allows a status to reflect a failure that happened mid-stream. gRPC isn't built on HTTP/2 for performance; it's built on it because HTTP/2's stream abstraction is the RPC abstraction.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Your gRPC service scales from 3 pods to 30 and latency doesn't improve. Diagnose it.

📍 Seen in the wild: the single most common gRPC production surprise, and it fails silently.

🎯 Really testing: whether you connect multiplexing to load distribution — the thing HTTP/2's efficiency costs you.

The clients are still talking to the original three pods. gRPC clients open a long-lived HTTP/2 connection and multiplex every RPC over it, so an L4 balancer — a Kubernetes ClusterIP Service using kube-proxy, an NLB, anything hashing the 4-tuple — makes exactly one decision per connection, at connection time. Twenty-seven new pods appear and receive nothing, because no client is opening a new connection. Every health check passes, no errors are logged, and aggregate latency creeps up as the original three saturate. The diagnostic is request rate per pod: a near-perfect 3-versus-27 split is unmistakable once you look, and invisible if you're watching cluster-level metrics.

Three fixes, and they're not equivalent. An L7 balancer (Envoy, an ALB, a gRPC-aware ingress) parses HTTP/2 frames and balances per-request, which is the general answer and the one that costs a proxy hop. Client-side load balancing — gRPC's own round_robin policy with a resolver that returns all backend addresses, or a headless Service in Kubernetes — has the client hold a connection to every backend and distribute across them, which removes the hop and is what a service mesh does under the hood. Connection age recycling (MAX_CONNECTION_AGE plus a grace period on the server) forces periodic reconnection so the balancer gets to decide again; it's the cheap mitigation and it belongs on regardless of which of the other two you pick, because it bounds how long a bad distribution can persist. The trade is a proxy hop versus client complexity versus a periodic reconnect blip, and picking one is a genuine architecture decision rather than a config lookup.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Approach Balances Cost When to pick it
L4 (ClusterIP, NLB) Connections Fails for gRPC — one connection, one backend Only if clients reconnect constantly
L7 proxy (Envoy, ALB) Individual RPCs An extra hop and its latency; a component to run The general default, especially with mixed clients
Client-side (round_robin) RPCs, from the client Client complexity; every client holds N connections Internal service-to-service where you own both ends
Service mesh sidecar RPCs, locally Sidecar CPU and memory per pod Already running a mesh; you get this free
MAX_CONNECTION_AGE Nothing directly — forces re-decisions Periodic reconnect blips Always on, alongside any of the above

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The mapping from gRPC concepts to HTTP/2 mechanisms is the thing to be able to recite:

gRPC concept HTTP/2 mechanism
One RPC One stream (client-initiated, odd ID)
Server / client / bidi streaming DATA frames over time on that one stream
Deadline cancellation RST_STREAM on that stream only
Status code returned after the body HTTP trailers (grpc-status)
Metadata HEADERS frames, HPACK-compressed
Backpressure on a streaming RPC HTTP/2 per-stream flow control

The skew arithmetic. With c client connections spread over n backends by an L4 balancer, expected load per backend is proportional to the connections it received — and with long-lived connections, c is small and fixed. 3 clients, 30 pods, L4: at most 3 pods receive traffic; 27 are idle regardless of request rate. The same 3 clients through an L7 proxy: all 30 share the RPCs. The failure scales with n ÷ c, so it gets worse the more you scale out — which is the opposite of the intuition that makes it hard to spot.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Don't put gRPC behind an L4 load balancer and consider it done. Traffic pins to whichever backends held connections at connection time, and scaling out makes the skew worse rather than better. Every health check passes while it happens, which is why it goes unnoticed for weeks.

  • Don't use gRPC for browser clients without a proxy. Browsers cannot control HTTP/2 frames directly, so gRPC-Web plus a translating proxy (Envoy's gRPC-Web filter) is required, and gRPC-Web does not support client or bidirectional streaming. If the browser needs true bidirectional streaming, WebSocket or SSE is the honest answer.

  • Don't run gRPC through middleboxes that downgrade to HTTP/1.1. An older WAF or proxy that terminates at 1.1 breaks gRPC outright — there is no fallback mode. This is a real constraint when introducing gRPC into an environment with an established edge tier.

  • Don't set MAX_CONNECTION_AGE aggressively low. Reconnection costs a handshake and a cold congestion window, and every reconnect is a small latency blip across every client. Minutes to tens of minutes, not seconds.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "gRPC uses HTTP/2 for performance."

✅ Reality: It uses HTTP/2 because HTTP/2's stream abstraction is the RPC abstraction — bidirectional streaming, per-call cancellation, per-call flow control and trailers all have no HTTP/1.1 expression. Performance is a consequence; the dependency is structural, which is why there is no HTTP/1.1 fallback.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): I assumed a Kubernetes Service load-balanced gRPC the way it balances HTTP/1.1 traffic. It doesn't — kube-proxy operates at L4, so it balances connections, and a gRPC client holds one long-lived connection. That single fact explains a whole category of "we scaled out and nothing improved" incidents, and it's the strongest practical reason to know how multiplexing interacts with load balancing rather than treating them as separate topics.

notes.title: Protocol Negotiation — ALPN and Alt-Svc
notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • ALPN — RFC 7301: TLS Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation Extension

  • Alt-Svc — RFC 7838: HTTP Alternative Services

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Which one picks HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2? ALPN, inside the TLS ClientHello. Costs zero extra round trips.
How does a client learn about HTTP/3? Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=... on an earlier response — used on the next connection.
The tokens? http/1.1, h2, h3.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Two mechanisms, for two different situations. ALPN is a TLS extension: the client lists the protocols it speaks (h2, http/1.1) in the ClientHello and the server picks one, so version selection is free — it rides a handshake that was happening anyway. That works for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 because both run over TCP. HTTP/3 runs over UDP, so a client can't offer it on a TCP connection it hasn't opened; instead the server advertises Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400 on an HTTP/2 response, and the client uses h3 on its next connection. That deferral is a deployment lever worth remembering: the ma value bounds how fast you can both roll out and roll back.
